subject: shoebill
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: shoebill stork.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I'm thinking about an unexpected artistic style for the shoebill stork—since it's a Nile swamp bird, something like ancient Egyptian tomb-painting with flat color, gold leaf, and lapis blue could be striking, though a Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock approach is also tempting.

I decide to go with "ancient Egyptian painted relief meets gilded funerary statuette": a lapis blue-grey body, gold bill with painted stripes, a turquoise beaded broad collar, and papyrus/feather-pattern decoration on the wings in lapis, turquoise, red, and gold. Now I'm sketching the actual skeleton structure, starting with the hip joint as root and planning realistic proportions based on the shoebill's true size—about 1.2m tall with a long, hooked bill and very long legs and toes.

I'm laying out the spine chain from pelvis through chest, a short thick S-curved neck up to a large head, then working out leg segment lengths (thigh, tibia, tarsus, toes) so the limb reaches the ground with a slight forward-bending knee typical of birds.

So the leg chain gets four named points: hip, knee, ankle, and footL as the tip. Now I need toes—three forward digits plus a hind hallux—each built as its own small chain branching from the foot joint.

Setting tarsus to end at the foot joint with toes starting forward at a slightly lower height, flat with small claw spikes using hexagonal sides. For wings, I'm weighing a fully folded rest pose against the guidance for extended wings, settling on a compromise where wings are held semi-open and drooped outward with a shoulder-elbow-wrist chain and fanned primary feathers.

I'll fan feathers out in rows along the trailing edge—primaries longest, then secondaries, coverts, and lesser feathers—each row an extruded leaf-shaped outline painted with Egyptian colors, roughly 33 feathers per wing for about 66 parts total across both wings.

For bone assignment, I'll pass primaries to the wrist joint, secondaries to the elbow/forearm joint, and coverts to the forearm, using explicit bone parameters per feather. For the arm chain, I'm working out the joint path from shoulder to elbow to wrist to hand tip, figuring out that a path of 4 points gives 3 spans, each span corresponding to one joint.

I'm now laying out actual wing coordinates for the left side -- shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand tip positions -- to define a half-open wing pose.

Then I'm planning the feather structure: secondaries attached along the elbow-to-wrist segment angled backward and slightly outward, roughly eight of them spaced evenly, with primaries fanning out from the hand tip.

I'm figuring out the coverts as shorter overlapping rows near the arm, then thinking about coloring the piece in an Egyptian painted style with the wing done in dark slate tones fading to paler tips, and layering in lapis and turquoise for the covert rows.

Setting the full Egyptian palette now, with ochre, gold, turquoise, lapis, cream, and kohl tones. For the body I'm leaning toward a rishi-style scale pattern across the lapis-slate feathers, lighter on top and darker underneath, to keep the countershading realistic while still feeling painterly rather than overly busy.

The massive bill itself I want gilded gold, sized to match the shoebill's bulbous hooked shape, with painted kohl and red stripe accents echoing an Egyptian funerary mask rather than the real horn-yellow mottling. I can pull a gilt metal material from the clockwork kit for that, and for the eyes I'm thinking a subtle glow with an Eye of Horus-style kohl line drawn in profile.

For the eyes I'll go forward-facing like a real shoebill's, built as yellow iris SVG decals with a kohl outline, extending into a Horus-style cosmetic line and falcon marking below, mirrored across the face. The head itself is an ellipsoid with a small nape tuft crest, eyes set forward on the sides, and the bill constructed as two separate mandibles -- I'm lofting the upper mandible from base to tip with varying width and height stations to get that bulging profile.

I'm defining the hooked nail tip, broad clog-like bill shape with a ridged culmen, and a shorter tucked-in lower mandible with gular area, attaching both to head and jaw bones through separate joints. I'm also working out the head position and bill angle so it points forward and down around 30 degrees, matching the real bird's posture.

Defining more bill loft stations...

I'm planning a gold base with mottled kohl-brown marbling streaks, a dark cutting-edge line between mandibles, and a subtle Egyptian chevron band near the bill base, keeping the palette restrained. The lower jaw gets its own loft running through stations from the base to the tip.

For the actual geometry, I'm bending the lower jaw downward with tapering width and height toward the tip, adding a visible gular pouch, and positioning the jaw joint relative to the head's local frame. I'm working out how to set the bone chain for the loft and settle on a reasonable section shape with moderate polygon sides for a low-poly but smooth look.

Now I'm laying out the neck chain from chest to head with three joints and a tapering radius sweep for that thick shoebill neck, then attaching the head joint to the end of the neck chain. Next I'm starting the spine chain for the body, defining hip root and spine points leading up toward the chest.

For the tail, I'll use three points curving back and down from the hips, named tail1-tail3, with a fan of seven feathers extruded from the tail2 bone, pointing backward and angled downward with a 0.3 length spread horizontally. Then I'm moving on to loft the torso body along the spine path.

I'm sweeping the body using a catmull-rom path from tail root through hips to chest, with an ellipse radius function varying rx/ry at several t-values to shape a tilted sausage form widening toward the chest and tapering at both ends.

Deciding the hips joint owns the path portion before it, with the spine chain extending from there, so I'll pass the bone as hips then spine. For the torso surface, I'm planning a scale pattern using cell noise, sourcing the right helper functions from the SDK to build the paint function.

Writing scale shading...

I'm layering a countershading effect between the darker back scales and a paler belly tone, aiming for that Egyptian painted-and-gilded look: slate-blue scale panels with turquoise feather-edge detailing on the chest, plus a gold usekh collar made of concentric beaded rings in turquoise, lapis, red, and gold with teardrop pendants around the neck base.

I'm figuring out how to build that collar as actual geometry -- cutting cross-sectional loops around the neck at different heights and sweeping colored bands along them, with a ring of small extruded teardrop beads on the outermost loop. It's a bit heavy computationally but should work, as long as it doesn't obscure the shoebill's face or break its silhouette.

Painting on the lathe by computing radial distance from the collar's center axis for the banded colors, plus scattering about fourteen small teardrop pendant drops along the rim. I also want to tilt the collar so it sits naturally sloping down at the front of the chest, following the neck's angle rather than sitting perfectly flat.

I'm sketching a shallow cone profile for the collar, floating slightly off the chest since Egyptian collars normally lie flat, and setting its tilted axis and base position at the neck to check it clears the body surface.

That's acceptable since the collar is covered by wings and feathers anyway, matching how real shoebill collars sit against the body. Now I'm positioning the eyes with a pale yellow decal on the front sides of the head, computing the placement offsets and the outward-facing direction vector for the decal so it reads correctly on the skull surface.

I'm placing the eye decal using a surface hit on the skull sphere with azimuth and elevation offsets, then adding a subtle glow to the pale yellow irises. Now I'm moving on to the eye artwork itself, sketching an almond-shaped kohl-lined Egyptian eye with an extended cosmetic line in an SVG viewbox.

I'll add a wedjat tear-line curling down from the eye's inner-lower corner, keeping the texture mostly transparent except for painted marks. For the head, I'm sizing the eyes to capture that iconic shoebill stare, then adding a small wispy nape crest made of five fanning leaf-shaped blades in lapis and gold, positioned toward the back-top of the head.

Shaping the feather outlines...

Designing color bands for wing feather paints...

Thinking about a cartouche decal on the flanks with simple pseudo-hieroglyphs—ankh, water lines, eye, feather, sun disc—arranged in a vertical column, plus tear-drop beads and maybe a lotus pattern on the leg bands, though some of these feel skippable for simplicity.

For remaining texture decisions: the tail gets painted feathers, the collar uses paint rather than beadwork texture, and bill markings can just be part of the base bill paint rather than a separate decal. For downy fluff at the thighs and belly, I'm thinking of using small plume-shaped cards with a lapis-to-turquoise gradient and kohl outline, scattered around 120 of them to break up the blocky silhouette while still counting as a single texture type.

I'm tallying up the part budget now — body, neck, head, collar with drops, bill components, eyes, crest, brow ridges, wing feathers and sweeps, tail, legs with toes and claws, plume cards, and decals — landing around 190 parts total, which fits my target range. Now I'm setting up the coordinate constants to start building everything concretely.

Working out the leg geometry: hip joints positioned on either side of the body, with foot targets straight below, and a three-segment chain (thigh, knee, ankle) sized so the total reach matches the real distance, with the knee bending forward and the ankle hinging back to mimic how a bird's leg actually articulates under its feathers.

Thinking about leg coloring in the stylized aesthetic—considering dark kohl-brown tones for the legs with possible gold or lapis accent details to tie into the decorative motif.

Still working out radius taper...

Now I'm planning the foot and toe geometry: ankle joint at the tarsus end, then three forward toes spread at roughly ±28° plus a backward-pointing hallux, with each toe built as a simple base-mid-tip chain scaled to shoebill-like proportions.

Adding claw spikes at each toe tip...

For wings, I'll parent them to the upper spine joint near the shoulder, positioning attachment points on both sides of the body. I'm plotting the wing shape with a T-pose-ish outward angle, defining shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand points with a sweep that thins from base to tip.

Now I'm working out feather orientation — since feathers should lie flat like horizontal blades, I need the width axis to be horizontal and perpendicular to each feather's direction, computing it as the cross product of the up vector with the direction vector so the thickness axis ends up roughly vertical.

Mirroring left and right feathers just flips the side vector, which is fine since the outline is symmetric. Now I'm laying out the secondary feather row, computing base positions by lerping between two wing points and setting direction and length values with slight overlap between feathers.

Overlapping flat feathers at the same height will cause z-fighting, so I'm adding small vertical offsets and alternating heights between neighboring feathers to separate them visually. Then I'm starting the primary feather row, varying angle and length along the wing to make the tips point outward properly.

Checking the math, the outermost primaries would push the wingspan beyond the real bird's proportions, so I'm shortening the primary length to keep the span closer to 2.4-2.6. I'm then laying out greater coverts along the arm with a curved path and slight outward tilt, followed by smaller lesser coverts and primary coverts that follow the same fan direction as the primaries but shorter.

Totaling the feathers gives roughly 43 per wing and 86 overall, matching my target count. I'm now binding each feather group to its proper bone -- secondaries to the elbow joint, primaries and their coverts to the wrist -- and sweeping the wing and neck chains with tapered radii, sharing the same lapis/scale paint instance for visual continuity between body and neck.

I'm working out a custom paint function that blends dark lapis and slate tones based on surface normal and a cellular pattern, trying to get pale countershading on the front of the neck and body without it looking too uniform.

Instead of overengineering this, I'll just reuse a prebuilt `scales` function nested inside `countershade`, feeding it slate/lapis tones with a kohl outline for the back and cream-grey tones for the belly, splitting them at a negative y-level threshold for a natural shading transition.

Now I'm setting up a concrete color palette as hex strings, covering kohl black, lapis blues, slates, cream, gold, turquoise, red, bone, and eye yellow. I'm starting on the bill's paint function, which streaks gold tones using layered noise sampling across the surface.

Adding the zigzag chevron stripe pattern...

For the hooked upper mandible, I'm shaping a downward-angled cone tip for the bill's nail, deciding whether to paint it dark for contrast against the gold. I'm settling on the overall bill proportions now—roughly a quarter-unit length and narrower width to match the shoebill's distinctive silhouette.

Now I'm plotting the bill's cross-section stations along its curve from the head joint outward, gradually narrowing the width and height toward the rounded tip before adding the nail spike angled downward and forward from the final station.

Next I'm defining the lower jaw stations under the bill, narrowing in width and depth as they run from near the head joint toward the tip, and calculating where the upper bill's lower edge sits relative to the jaw.

I'll skip the gular pouch but add a lower jaw bottom with gold accents, plus a jaw joint connecting the head to the mandible tip. For the mouth line I'm considering a thin dark kohl gap, and along the upper mandible I want a lighter gold ridge sweeping along the culmen, with two kohl nostril slits near the top.

Working out nostril placement, I'm computing where the bill's elliptical cross-section puts the surface height at a given forward position, then placing small flattened kohl spheres symmetrically on either side of the ridge, embedded slightly into the surface -- possibly snapping them onto the bill mesh directly rather than computing coordinates by hand.

For head details, I'm adding a brow ridge with Egyptian-style kohl/lapis eyebrow lines, planning to fold this into the existing eye decal as a cosmetic arc rather than building a separate geometric sweep. For skull coloring, I'm considering slate tones with pale cheek accents and scale-like paint patterns.

Now for the crest, I'm working out a small tuft of blades extending off the back of the head, figuring out the base position and spread directions for 5 feather-like protrusions, and debating whether the blade plane should lie flat or vertical for a crest pointing backward -- I'll add a `side` parameter to the helper to control the orientation.

For the tail, I'm planning 7 feathers fanning out horizontally from the base near tail1/tail2, spread roughly ±40° with slight downward angle, each 0.3 long and 0.08 wide, alternating heights for a natural fan look, and starting to sketch out the plume card shapes.

Still writing SVG...

Adding more glyph shapes for the cartouche -- ankh loop, water zigzags, feather, eye, reed lines -- styled as kohl ink on a cream background with a gold border and red rim, placed as a flank decal around mid-body height where it stays visible below the spread wings. Considering a chest emblem or leg-band texture but leaning toward skipping those to keep things simple.

Deciding to skip the wing-arm stripe and a scarab emblem, settling on a core texture set of eye, cartouche, and two plume types, plus maybe a lotus motif. I'm leaning toward adding a small blue lotus ornament sitting on the crown of the head above the bill, since it keeps the face unobstructed while adding a nice Egyptian decorative touch, alongside collar teardrop pendants rendered as simple two-color extruded shapes.

Setting glow for the eye decal. Now I'll start writing the actual TypeScript implementation, importing the geometry and shading helper functions I'll need for limbs, scales, gradients, and texture effects...

Setting up the builder with a 2048 paint size, then starting the skeleton by creating the hips joint as the root spine joint.

Next I'm building the spine as a short catmull-rom chain with two spans up to the chest, then continuing with a neck chain running from the top of the spine up to the head area with three segments.

For the neck curve, I'm giving it a slight S-shape, curving back then forward toward where the head will attach. Then I'm placing the head joint at the end of the neck with a slight forward/downward orientation, computing a local center point for the skull, and starting to build the skull geometry as a sphere.

Setting up the jaw joint...

Now I'm starting the bill as a loft shape anchored to head-local coordinates...

Still writing bill ridge geometry...

I'm adding the hook spike at the bill tip, then building the lower mandible loft reusing the bill paint palette for consistency, and sketching a flattened gular pouch sphere beneath the lower jaw.

For the mouth seam, I'm trying to approximate a thin kohl-colored line where the upper and lower bill meet, but the geometry is getting too fiddly to compute precisely from the station points, so I'm considering just skipping it or using a rough drape surface instead.

Writing seam line code...

Now placing the eye decals and a crown lotus decal on top of the skull, orienting the lotus to face forward with the up vector set to the forward direction, then positioning the eyes using spherical coordinates near the front sides of the skull.

I realize the eye position overlaps with the bill's width -- since the bill is nearly as wide as the head at that forward distance, the eye center ends up sitting inside the bill rather than above it. I need to raise the eye height so it clears the bill's top edge relative to the head crown.

Checking the eye position relative to the bill edge, the eye sits just outside the bill side, though the decal might get partially hidden where it overlaps the bill base—so I'll narrow the bill at its base to avoid clipping, and nudge the eye azimuth to 65. Now I'm moving on to the collar, setting up a lathe shape with a center and tilted axis near the neck.

Designing the collar outline, I'm tracing an outer curve from the top down to the rim, then back along the underside to close the loop into a thin shell without self-intersection.

Now I'm working out the paint logic for the lathe, computing radial distance from the axis at each point and mapping bands of that radius to different colors like gold, kohl, turquoise, and lapis for the collar's decorative rings.

For the outer bands I'm alternating turquoise and lapis in angular blocks to create a beaded pattern, using an angle-based index with modulo parity to decide block colors, which requires setting up orthonormal basis vectors perpendicular to the axis. I'm also planning the 18 teardrop drops hanging from the rim, positioning each one using the axis and angle offset combined with the basis vectors.

Working out the drop placements along the collar rim at radius .222, hanging downward-outward from the slope direction near the lower surface, keeping them thin at .008 thickness so they read as hanging droplets off the rim edge.

Then I realize the collar at radius .22 is way too large relative to the .12-wide body — it'd occlude the wing roots at (±0.12, 0.84). I decide to scale the whole outline down by a factor of 0.8, bringing the outer rim to about .178, and reposition it so it sits properly covering the front of the chest relative to the .062 neck base radius.

With the scaled inner collar radius at about .05, that's smaller than the neck sweep radius of .07 at its base, which means the neck will pass through and hide the join nicely. Now I'm working out the geometry of the tilted cone axis to figure out where the front rim of the collar lands against the chest surface, calculating the perpendicular radial direction and projecting the rim point forward and down from the center.

Checking the result, the front rim ends up sticking out about 8cm beyond the body's chest surface at that height, which means it's floating rather than sitting flush. For the back rim though, projecting along the opposite radial direction, that point lands inside the body outline, so the collar fits there.

Given this mismatch, I'm reconsidering the collar axis orientation — tilting it more forward so it hugs the chest surface better, then re-deriving the front rim position with the new axis and comparing it against sampled points along the body's torso path.

Rather than let the collar float, I accept it may sit as a stiff gorget slightly ahead of the chest, recalculating with K=0.7 and the rim radius at .155, checking both the front and side rim positions against the body's width to see how much clearance remains.

Now I'm setting up the tail chain as three joints following a curved path, with seven tail feathers fanning horizontally from the base at angles between -35° and 35°, alternating heights and extruding each as a flat plane oriented by the local up-cross-forward direction.

For the body sweep, I'm deciding which bones it should span—thinking through whether the tail root overlaps with the hips segment and settling on including tail, hips, and spine bones together since bone order doesn't matter. I'm now working out the radius function along the body length, checking the sine curve values at each parameter to make sure the shape doesn't balloon too large near the start.

Still writing radius function...

Using LAPIS_DK for coverts. Now I'm sketching a feather-row builder that samples points along the arm's catmull path by parameter t, pulling base positions from the path rather than the joint chain directly, with elbow and wrist references coming from the arm's joints array for orientation.

I'm building a cached paint function that colors each feather based on its normalized position along its length, keeping a thin quill line down the center, a tip color near the end, a kohl accent band just before that, and an optional secondary band partway along, falling back to the base color elsewhere.

I'm realizing the cache key would explode across ~60 feather variants since the pattern depends on normalized distance (u = s[0]/L), so I'm considering switching to absolute distance from the tip instead so the paint function can be cached independently of each feather's length.

For color assignment per row, I'm mapping out an Egyptian palette scheme: primaries alternating lapis-dark/lapis with gold tips, secondaries lapis base with gold/turquoise tips, greater coverts turquoise base with light gold tips, and lesser coverts with slate tones for the body.

I'm deciding the lesser coverts should be slate base with lapis tips to keep continuity with the shoebill's grey body, then mid coverts lapis base with turquoise tips, and greater/secondary rows progressing to gold-tipped flight feathers for a striking but cohesive gradient from shoulder to wingtip. I'm also staggering the row heights slightly (lesser +0.03, mid +0.02, greater +0.01, secondaries flush) to avoid z-fighting between overlapping feather planes.

Now I'm building the leg chains symmetrically for left and right, placing hip joints below the body and generating three-segment limbs (hip, knee, ankle, foot) with proper parenting and contact points for the feet.

Still refining leg paint logic...

Now I'm adding gold anklet rings on the tarsus using torus geometry aligned to the leg's tangent and bone, plus a heel sphere at the ankle joint to sell the joint bulge. Then I'm starting on the toes, looping through a few splay angles to place each digit.

Working out toe placement...

Counting up the joint totals across toes, legs, wings, and tail to confirm the full skeleton stays manageable at around 50 joints, making sure feather bones get properly weighted. Now I'm planning surface scatter cards for body, neck, and thigh skin texture with distance and normal filtering.

Tuning the feather card sizes and bend parameters so density stays balanced without covering the base body paint — settling on roughly 90 cards on the body, 40 on the neck, 30 on the thighs. I'm confirming the eye decal and glow effect will work correctly with the mesh part structure, then starting to draft the SVG for the eye shape itself.

Writing SVG code...

Still designing the eye and kohl markings...

Now I'm sketching the cartouche shape: a rounded rectangle outline with a horizontal bar at the base representing the knot, and inside I'm placing symbolic glyphs—a sun disc, wavy lines, an ankh, and a feather stacked vertically.

Still writing glyph shapes...

Writing feather plume SVGs...

I'm now counting out the texture set so far and thinking about adding a sixth: a small winged scarab medallion decal applied to the collar's lathe surface, with a lapis body and gold wing arcs.

Placing the scarab decal onto the collar's front outer surface, aimed forward-up from center, using a raycast hit against the conical collar shape with a size guard in case the hit misses. Now defining helper functions and a feather-generation routine for building the wing geometry...

Writing feather outline coordinates...

Setting smoothing and a tiny bevel to keep edges safe, then starting the wing-building loop with shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand points for each side...

I'm defining the arm chain with sweep thickness tapering toward the tip, and now deciding which joints should drive secondaries, primaries, and coverts for feather attachment.

For coverts I'm splitting attachment between elbow and wrist based on position along the feather row, then computing secondary feather bases by interpolating between elbow and wrist with varying length to approximate real wing proportions.

I'm now adjusting lengths and height offsets per feather using an alternating/cyclic pattern so neighboring feathers don't overlap unnaturally, checking spacing against feather width to catch collisions with feathers two or three positions away.

Now I'm shifting to the primaries, working out their angle and length as a function of position along the wing, interpolating angle outward from the wrist and varying length so the middle-outer primaries come out longest.

Working out covert row placement and tilt...

Total parts land around 98+, which feels reasonable. The lesser coverts tuck into the arm's leading edge so their bases stay hidden near the top of the arm radius, skipping the alula for simplicity since the tail and back are already covered by the wings. I'm also adding a small nape crest tuft made of five blades spreading outward from the back of the skull.

Giving the crest blades a lapis-dark base fading to gold tips, keeping them thin and wispy. I'm skipping a gold lappet addition for now, and double-checking that the whole model stands correctly with the toes resting at ground level.

Writing the bill paint logic to add gilt metal striping with kohl and chevron turquoise/cream bands...

Mapping out the bill bands more precisely: KOHL stripes bracketing a chevron section near the widest part, then adding a noise-driven streak pattern beyond the band region that blends in rusty and dark kohl-brown tones over the base gilt color.

For the collar, I'm setting up a cylindrical coordinate system around a central point and axis, converting each paint sample point into local radius and angle values so I can divide the collar into discrete angular segments for banding — this runs during the initial build before any pose transforms are applied.

Now I'm mapping out concentric radius bands for the collar design: a gold rim, kohl separator lines, and alternating bead rows cycling between turquoise/lapis and red/gold colors based on angular segment, building outward toward a petal-decorated gold band.

I'm also working out the undersurface shading using the surface normal's dot product with the vertical axis to darken faces pointing downward, plus deciding on 36 bead columns and 18 pendant drops cycling between lapis and turquoise colors with flat shading.

Now I'm computing the drop placement geometry — figuring out local radial and tangential basis vectors at each angle so I can position the drop base near the collar's underside rim and orient its slope and thickness correctly in 3D.

With the drop count and placement sorted, I'm moving on to positioning the scarab decal on the collar's front face, using an angular offset around the collar's center.

Writing SVG code...

Still working through the facial feature placement, checking how surface hit detection and decal positioning APIs apply to the eyes and skull geometry before finalizing the code.

That stretches too much near silhouette, so I'll pull the eye placement more frontal using az 40, el 30 instead, recalculating the sphere point and bill width to keep the eye decal within the bill's bounds.

Still working out the overlap—the eye's bottom edge dips below the bill's top edge, getting hidden. I'll try lowering the bill stations and shrinking the base width slightly, then reposition the eye at el 38, az 48 to get it sitting properly above the bill base.

Finishing the bill stations and adding the lower mandible profile, I'm checking overlap between upper and lower curves at matching points to confirm the bill closes naturally without gaps.

I'm placing the hook tip below the bill and then working out nostril placement relative to the bill surface height at a given point.

Now I'm building the seam line between upper and lower bill halves, computing offset coordinates at each station and tapering toward the tip, then setting up a curve through those points with a small radius for the bone structure.

I'm setting up plume card scatter with texture variation, naming the body sweep "torso", and adding thigh scattering filtered to the lower leg region. I need to double-check unused imports won't trip up the typechecker's strict settings before finalizing the code.

Writing import statements and palette constants...

Still defining color palettes...

Building the torso spine curve with keyframed radius interpolation...

Working out the tail sweep geometry and feather placement along the tail path...

Writing feather paint caching logic...

I'll type the map explicitly to avoid implicit-any issues, and tighten the quill line width slightly to 0.0028 for better texel coverage. Now I'm writing a feather helper function that builds the barb geometry from a base point, direction, length, width, and color, with optional lift and thickness parameters.

Verifying the cross-product math...

Working out the direction vector for feather placement using sine and cosine of the angle, then figuring out how to map a position parameter along the arm path to the correct bone segment—shoulder, elbow, or wrist—so each feather attaches rigidly to the right joint.

For the legs, I'm sweeping the leg geometry per side with a defined radius and color, then adding ankle bulge details and small decorative rings along the tarsus using torus shapes at specific positions with gold and red coloring.

Now I'm defining the toe geometry, setting up three toes (inner, middle, outer) with varying lengths and widths positioned at the end of each leg's path.

Each toe is built as a chain of three segments branching off the foot's tip, with named joints feeding into a tip frame for attaching claws next.

I'll name it `toeBack${sd}` and skip the toe web detail. For the leg, I'm setting the chain parented to hips with four polyline points, deriving side from joint x-position, and adding foot padding plus thigh fluff cards before composing everything together with the metadata. Now I'm writing a helper for outlined glyph strokes using double-layered SVG paths.

Still designing the cartouche graphic...

The glow function uses each texture's emissive map, so textured parts like kohl will keep their own dark coloring since emissive derives from the map color itself.

I'm skipping verdigris metal detailing and finalizing the assembly: building a skull sphere part for the head surface, adding scattered neck ruff cards, placing an eye cheek decal, and positioning a lotus at the crown using the hit normal for direction with upward orientation and small scale. I'm checking build order and noting a potential decal placement issue to resolve.

Now I'm writing out the full file, aiming for roughly 600 lines with reasonably typed helpers like a local-coordinate function for head positioning and a neck sweep radius function that tapers over a parameter, keeping everything consistent with the plumage color scheme.

Checking the neck-to-head connection point and radius, confirming the spine joints parent correctly to the neck, and verifying skull part scaling. Setting up the collar lathe geometry with its outline, axis, bone attachment, and segment count before finalizing the write.

Now I'm writing a loop that places 18 small drop shapes evenly around the collar, computing each drop's angle, position, and orientation to extrude a thin blade-like shape colored cyclically, parented to the neck bone. I note that drops at the back of the collar will be hidden inside the body, which is fine since that region is already occluded.

I'm defining the drop's cross-section as a pointed teardrop polygon and checking the scaling so they hang slightly past the collar rim, then double-checking the random seed usage for scattering decorative elements across the neck surface, confirming sweep sides options before finalizing the build.

Now I'm writing the top-level descriptive comment establishing the piece's style as gilded Egyptian tomb-painting funerary art.
